Three traps, and they're all false friends: «ich will» means "I want", never "I will"; «ich muss nicht» means "I don't have to", not "I must not"; and «ich darf nicht» is the real "I mustn't / I'm not allowed".
Können: o primeiro verbo modal, passo a: Können: your first modal verb, step by step
Um verbo MODAL ajuda outro verbo a dizer: A MODAL verb helps another verb say "can", "must", "should", "want to". Let's build the first one, «können» — a cousin of English "can". STEP 1: «können» says what you know how to do or are able to do: «Ich kann schwimmen» = I can swim. STEP 2: conjugate «können»; it's irregular in the singular: ich kann, du kannst, er kann, wir können, ihr könnt, sie können. STEP 3: the second verb goes to the END of the sentence, in the infinitive: «Ich kann gut schwimmen» — "I can well swim". The sentence is "bracketed": the modal in 2nd position and the infinitive at the end. STEP 4: to ask, the modal goes to the front: «Kannst du schwimmen?» — exactly like "Can you swim?". STEP 5: to negate, «nicht» goes before the verb at the end: «Ich kann nicht schwimmen.» RULE OF THUMB: «ich» and «er» are the SAME (kann) and never take -t — just as English says "I can, he can", never "he cans".
o português também usa «saber» ou «poder: English modals work almost the same way: "I can swim", "Can you swim?", and "he can" with no -s, just like «er kann» with no -t. The one big difference is position: in German, the infinitive always goes to the END of the sentence instead of staying next to the modal. «Ich kann sehr gut Deutsch sprechen» — "I can very well German speak".

With «er», the modal takes no -t — like "he can", not "he cans".
The main verb goes to the END of the sentence.
